FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE October 15, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-1 At the October 1, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: New Interdisciplinary Minor in Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities: We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities. The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone. Other sources include access and equality. Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities.
The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone.
Other sources include access and equality.
Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them.
More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process.
We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.
Course options for the minor represent an array of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches to social justice topics.
Students who complete the
3 minor will emerge with a nuanced understanding of the world around them, the

4 reasons why people continue to seek to change that world, and a familiarity with the organizing tools and strategies available to those efforts.
A core intellectual component of the minor is an emphasis on seeing the world through the lens of other people's experiences, especially people and groups who have different social, racial, ethnic, economic, religious, gendered, and geographic backgrounds from one's own.
Developing a critical consciousness of the intersections of one's identities, privileges, and power is another important component.
This can lead to more compassionate and meaningful relationships with others.
Moreover, a deep understanding of one's positionality can help perpetuate or dismantle systems and structures that ultimately impact minoritized communities.
Students will learn about subtle and blatant institutional barriers and the micro-aggressions that systematically oppress people.
Students will have experiential learning opportunities that allow them to see the ways in which the ideas they read about and discuss in class actually play out in the real world.

Students will engage in civic processes visiting with community leaders, activists, and politicians to influence policies.
They will prepare for and engage in civic processes reflecting on these experiences.
They will learn theories, methods, and skills that they can use in their work and personal lives to improve the human condition.
Courses for the minor are organized into three categories; peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills, and students are required to take at least one course from each category (and not more than three) and then complete their credit requirements in consultation with advisors.
An ongoing advisory committee of faculty, staff, and peers will meet once per semester to review advising strategies, and tweak the course offerings, making sure that courses are still being offered, that faculty who teach them are informed about the minor, and review new course options that become available to include in the minor.
The committee will also develop and distribute marketing materials for the minor and maintain a Google work site for students who pursue the minor and for faculty and staff who contribute to it.

This site will also serve to inform the community about experiential learning opportunities that arise in the interest of social justice and civic responsibilities.
Currently, the committee includes several faculty, staff, and undergraduate students.
